Area.evidence_source: [page/3/Text/6] As gay children, and not yet able to identify themselves as such, the boys had an awareness of being different, of knowing, but this appeared to be a 'felt' knowing and not a knowing they could articulate.[page/3/Text/9] The participants' knowing, having the ability to verbalize their difference in terms of their sexuality, gave rise to an increased sense of vulnerability.[page/3/Text/10] For me, that was probably one of the most terrible phases of my life. That was one of the absolute lowest points... really horrible. I can still very, very vividly remember just sitting on my own and for a couple of days I didn't talk to anybody. I suppose looking back now, it was a way of saying I'm hurting so much please notice that. (Carl)[page/3/Text/11] As teenagers, the knowing equated to becoming conscious of their unacceptability, giving rise to self-doubt and vulnerability.[page/3/Text/12] That was a terrible time [moving schools], those teenage years, and on top of that, as I was becoming sort of 12, 13, sexually aware and the whole gay thing starting to kick in . . . it was a cry for help [started taking illegal drugs]. I'm saying I don't know where I stand as far as who loves me, and I mean, I feel vulnerable. (Ben)
